name: Textured PEI (powder-coated spring steel)
summary: The modern default build surface: PEI resin electrostatically powder-coated and cured onto stainless or spring steel, leaving a fine sandy micro-texture instead of a laminated film. The texture raises contact area while lowering peak bond strength, so it grips hot and self-releases cold across PLA, PETG, ABS and ASA with no adhesives — at the cost of a matte, slightly orange-peel print bottom.
surface_makeup: Polyetherimide (PEI) powder coating, electrostatically applied and thermoset onto a stainless or spring steel sheet (aluminium on budget plates); micro-texture is inherent to the powder coat, not embossed

filament_compatibility.notes: Excellent general result, though very aggressive textures can let thin or small PLA parts lift at the corners — add a brim for those.

preparation: On first use, wipe off factory handling oils with IPA or wash with warm soapy water and dry fully. Routine prep is a cold 90%+ IPA wipe before each print. The texture holds oils in its valleys more stubbornly than a smooth film does, so IPA alone gradually stops working — when first-layer adhesion degrades despite a fresh wipe, that is the signal for a warm soap-and-water deep clean rather than more alcohol. Handle by the tabs, keep fingers off the print area, and re-run first-layer calibration when switching from a smooth or satin sheet, since the effective Z datum differs. Textured PEI is more forgiving of a slightly high nozzle than smooth is, which makes it the easier surface for a first Z-offset tune.
cleaning: Routine: cold IPA wipe with a lint-free cloth. Deep: warm water and unscented dish soap with a soft sponge, worked over the whole surface, then rinsed and dried completely before remounting so no water is trapped against the steel. Do not use acetone — Prusa explicitly warns it deteriorates the coating. Do not use metal scrapers, blades or wire brushes: they catch on the texture and gouge the powder coat, and gouges become permanent adhesion dead-zones. Baked-on filament residue from a Z-offset crash is best removed by warming the bed to that material's bed temperature and lifting it with a plastic scraper.
model_removal: This surface is designed to self-release. Let the plate cool to room temperature and most prints audibly pop free on their own as the steel and coating contract away from the printed polymer; lifting the sheet off the magnet and flexing it finishes the job for anything still attached. Reserve a plastic spatula for stubborn corners and brimmed prints, and slide it in at a shallow angle rather than levering. Never remove parts hot — the bond peaks at temperature and forcing it there is how the powder coat gets pulled off. Note that once a print pops loose during cooling it cannot be resumed, so paused or interrupted jobs need to be kept at bed temperature.
stuck_print_recovery: The freezer trick works quickly and reliably here: put the sheet with the print attached into a freezer for 10-15 minutes and flex it afterwards. For stubborn PETG or ABS footprints, drip 90%+ IPA at the part/plate interface and let it wick under the perimeter for a minute before flexing again. Unwaxed dental floss or thin wire sawed under a corner and drawn across the footprint is a gentle mechanical assist that will not damage the coating. Prints that do not release on the first cool-down — common with ASA and PC, where the sheet holds residual heat unevenly — usually free up after a full reheat to bed temperature followed by an undisturbed slow cool. Avoid ice or cold water directly on a hot plate.
lifespan_notes: Roughly 12-18 months of regular use before the texture wears smooth in the high-traffic centre of the plate, per Bambu-ecosystem community reporting. The classic wear symptom is zonal: prints stick fine at the edges and fail in the middle. Wear is accelerated by metal-tool scraping, acetone and other solvents, long ABS/ASA runs at high bed temperature, and baked-on filament from bad Z-offsets. The powder coat is not field-recoatable — some vendors re-coat returned sheets, but for most users the plate is a consumable to be replaced.

price.notes: Prusa textured powder-coated steel sheet about USD 40; Bambu Textured PEI Plate about USD 29 (unverified current price); FYSETC/BIQU double-sided textured+smooth sheets USD 20-30 in 235-310 mm sizes.

additional_notes: Community consensus rates this the single most forgiving general-purpose surface for mixed PLA/PETG/ABS work without adhesives — the trade-offs are a matte, slightly rough print bottom and less precise Z-datum control than smooth PEI. Commonly sold double-sided with a smooth or satin reverse, and magnetically mounted across essentially every modern consumer printer. Bambu ships it as the default plate on the X1, P1 and A1 series.

provenance.conflicts: No manufacturer publishes a hard maximum bed temperature for powder-coated PEI; Bambu rates its Textured PEI Plate across PLA through ABS and PETG-CF without a high-temp designation, so the 130 degC ceiling recorded here is inferred from supported material ranges rather than a datasheet figure. Nylon is contested: some plate vendors advertise textured PEI as nylon-compatible, while Prusa and the bulk of community experience push users to G10/garolite — recorded as avoid. Polycarbonate is likewise contested: forum reports of successful PC on textured FYSETC sheets exist alongside reports of coating pull-out, so it is recorded as usable-with-prep. PLA is occasionally reported to lift on very aggressive textures, which conflicts with its otherwise universal 'recommended' status. Bambu's USD 29 plate price is unverified against the manufacturer store.
